Watch: People shouldn't be punished for working harder, Badenoch says

Published 3 October 2026

Kemi Badenoch has said a Conservative government would scrap the "cliff edge" that means parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than £100,000 a year.

Speaking to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, the Conservative Party leader said: "What we want to see is that people who work harder don't get punished for doing so."

The earnings limit means only families where no parent earns more than this threshold are eligible for 30 hours of government-funded childcare or tax-free childcare.

The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham.

Badenoch, who arrived in the city on Saturday, has vowed the party was new and different from the one that lost the 2024 general election.

The Conservatives - who have been polling behind Labour and Reform UK over the past year - are expected to use the four-day event to lay out more of their policy agenda ahead of the next general election.

Ahead of the conference, the Conservatives produced a 100-page essay setting out their principles , external including a "central" belief that business, rather than governments, create growth.

It argues that governments should create the conditions for growth, particularly through the tax system.

In her interview with the BBC, Badenoch pitched herself as a "classic old-school Conservative" adding: "I believe in common sense - people working hard and being rewarded for that effort."

She insisted the Tories would keep the state pension triple lock, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to change if Labour wins the next election.

She said the policy, under which state pensions rise each year by the highest of inflation, average wages, or 2.5%, was "the right policy for pensioners".

She added: "What we don't want to see is people going after the elderly, chasing after vulnerable and disabled people, and then the extremely large cohort of people who can work, who are not working, are left alone."

The Conservatives have long called on the government to cut the growing welfare budget including by implementing tighter restrictions on claimants.

'Wrong choices'

The party said its childcare announcement would be a "first step" in broader efforts to address issues in the tax system which damage incentives to work or invest.

This will be a theme of shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith's conference speech on Monday.

Since September 2025, working parents in England have been entitled to 30 hours of free childcare , external for children aged between nine months and four years old.

However, to qualify both parents must earn less than £100,000 a year, although all three and four-year-olds are eligible for 15 hours of free childcare, regardless of parental income.

The same £100,000 eligibility threshold also applies to the government's tax-free childcare scheme , external , and has remained unchanged since it was originally set under the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government.

For every £8 paid into an online childcare account, the government adds £2, up to £2,000 per child per year, which parents can then use to pay for childcare.

The Tories said that if they return to power, they would remove the £100,000 threshold entirely for tax-free childcare and government-funded childcare hours.

The threshold has been criticised by economists, who point out it can leave parents worse off overall even after a pay rise of tens of thousands of pounds.

In her interview with Kuenssberg, Badenoch said: "What we want to see is more people in work and not taking the wrong decisions or the wrong choices, and it doesn't matter whether they're earning £10,000 or £100,000 - what matters is that people are out there working".

Asked if this could result in someone who earns £1m a year getting free childcare under a Conservative government, the Tory leader responded: "It doesn't matter what you earn - we don't want you to be punished for working hard. What we're trying to do is grow our economy."

What does childcare cost and how do government-funded hours work in England? Published 21 May

Education secretary to ask competition watchdog to review hidden childcare costs Published 25 May

Tories aim to be election-ready ahead of party conference Published 3 days ago

The Tories argue the threshold may mean some people may delay having children until their incomes change, or decide not to start a family at all, describing scrapping it as "both pro-family and pro-growth".

By providing an increased incentive to work, the Tories said the move would also boost economic growth.

They added that it would tackle the "unfairness" that the threshold is calculated on an individual earner's income rather then for the whole household.

The party said the policy would be funded by cutting the number of public servants working in "executive non-departmental public bodies" - organisations which have a role in the processes of national government but operate at arm's length from ministers, such as Arts Council England and the Environment Agency.

It said this would save £1.6bn by 2029-30, covering the estimated £700m cost of removing the childcare "cliff edge".

stories.title: Five reasons India's stock market is sinking even when its economy is growing
stories.summary: The world's fastest growing major economy has one of the worst performing major equity markets in 2026.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
India has one of the world's worst performing major equity markets in 2026

Published 2 hours ago

India's economy is growing at an enviable rate of over 7% despite global energy shocks, rising interest rates, tariff uncertainties and weather-related disruptions.

But the world's fastest growing major economy also has one of the worst performing major equity markets in 2026. The correction in Indian stocks has, in fact, only intensified in recent weeks.

The benchmark Sensex and Nifty indices, which represent the country's largest companies, have inched up slightly since Monday after posting losses for eight straight weeks - the longest losing streak in 25 years, according to Reuters.

Indian mom-and-pop investors who put their money into the Nifty have seen their wealth erode by about 15% this year. In comparison, they would have made 62% returns on Korea's Kospi index since January or 170% in the last two years.

On aggregate, the money foreign investors have put into Indian markets in the past decade - after subtracting what they sold or withdrew - is nearing zero. In the past two years alone, foreign institutional investors have withdrawn a staggering $40bn, according to data from Bernstein Research.

It is the large pool of domestic institutional and retail money, flowing into instruments like mutual funds, that have helped the markets avoid a sharper fall.

Domestic assets under management of mutual funds have grown from about $125bn in 2016 to some $900bn this year, with the number of Indians parking money in stocks and mutual funds more than tripling to 150 million individuals.

This makes the recent fall in the markets more worrying - since households, already struggling from a weak job market, high inflation and faltering consumption, are now seeing their equity savings take a beating too.

So, what's gone wrong?

Here are five reasons India's booming economy isn't lifting its stock market.

India imports over 90% of its crude requirements

Persistent energy shocks due to Middle East conflict

Crude oil prices have hovered between $90 and $100 a barrel as the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz enters its eighth month, far longer than analysts had expected. Moreover, there's little visibility on when normalcy will return.

"This single variable tends to influence the markets quite negatively," Hari Shyamsunder, a fund manager with Franklin Templeton Asset Management India, told the BBC. "Markets can absorb crude between $70 and $90, but when prices move above $100 a barrel, it starts putting stress on macro-economic variables such as inflation and also company earnings and margins."

India imports over 90% of its requirements - nearly half of its crude oil imports, along with a large share of its liquified petroleum gas (LPG) and liquified natural gas (LNG) shipments, come through the Strait of Hormuz.

While Delhi has diversified its energy sources, tapping Russian oil markets, US President Donald Trump recently threatened up to 100% tariffs on countries doing trade with Moscow, further complicating matters.

Rising global interest rates

With oil prices rising, inflation is going up and, as a result, interest rates are on the rise globally. The effective yield on US government bonds is above 5%, or at near 25-year highs.

These are often considered risk-free investments. As a result, foreign money tends to leave riskier emerging market assets such as Indian equities and chase safer investments like US bonds when interest rates rise.

Falling rupee

For foreign investors, the problem of muted returns has been compounded by a weaker rupee. In currency-adjusted dollar terms, they have suffered because of the fall in the Indian currency.

The Nifty has delivered just 6% annualised dollar returns over the past decade - hardly attractive, especially in comparison with several other competing markets.

Indian stocks are still expensive relative to their earnings compared to other emerging markets

Indian stocks are cheaper, but still relatively expensive

Stock valuations have been another major concern.

The market correction over the last two years has reduced the premium that Indian stocks held over their emerging market competitors.

"Stocks are cheaper than they have been on average for the last ten years," says Shyamsunder, adding that the premium that Indian shares commanded over other emerging economies has shrunk substantially in the past few years.

However, they are still expensive relative to their earnings, especially since companies in countries such as South Korea and Taiwan have benefited from a huge boom in artificial intelligence (AI) which has pushed up their profits.

The missing AI piece

In India, AI, or the new economy broadly, is a major missing piece of its growth story.

"Many of India's large caps [big companies] represent a bygone economic era," Bernstein Research said in a note recently. "Most are not investing in the future, but consolidating their past, often expecting policy to continue shielding them from global competition."

India seeks AI breakthrough - but is it falling behind?

And its smaller companies are yet to reach a scale that will attract foreign institutional funds.

While Indian companies are investing in data centres and chip fabrication, the country has not produced a global giant like OpenAI, Anthropic or even China's DeepSeek - this is where the largest share of the profits in the AI value chain lie.

Foreign investor interest will only return to India meaningfully if it can build globally competitive industries in these emerging areas, according to Bernstein.

"We are seeing early signs of this in areas such as space, defence, semiconductors, and deep-tech innovation, but most remain too small to materially influence capital allocation decisions over much of this decade."

Domestic savings into mutual funds haven't reduced despite the market correction

So what's next?

There are many immediate factors that will influence how Indian markets behave going forward.

"Easing geopolitical tensions and relatively attractive valuations could support a revival in FPI [foreign portfolio investor] inflows," according to CareEdge, a brokerage, though trade tensions and higher energy prices remain a “challenge for corporate performance going ahead”.

For now, while foreign investors may have given up, Indian savers, even though increasingly more anxious, haven't slowed their monthly investment flows , external into mutual funds.

The real test will be whether this resilience survives a deeper correction in the future.

stories.body:
Decision by Paramount Skydance executive David Ellison was relief to employees who feared overhaul – and possibility of Bari Weiss taking over

Mark Thompson, who since 2023 has served as chair and chief executive of CNN after a storied career in British and American media, will retain his role even after Paramount Skydance takes control of the company, he announced in a memo to network staffers on Monday morning.

While Thompson wrote that the “specifics of how CNN will plug into and operate in the new company have yet to be finalized”, he offered some pledges about his role at the combined company, which will be led by David Ellison, the Paramount Skydance chief executive, after the company merges with CNN parent company Warner Bros Discovery. The deal is expected to formally close on Tuesday.

“First, I’m convinced that from David Ellison on down, Paramount Skydance leadership really does believe in news alongside entertainment as a top strategic opportunity for our new company,” Thompson wrote. “They’ve seen our digital strategy and are as excited about it as we are.

“And second, having now spoken to them at length on the topic, I have real confidence that they both understand and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for. That’s why I will be leading CNN into this new chapter as it becomes one of Skydance’s suite of major media assets and global brands, and leading it as an independent editor-in-chief with the same responsibilities and prerogatives that I have now.”

The decision by Paramount Skydance leadership will bring relief to many CNN employees who feared a complete overhaul of the network. Some employees had also shared concerns that Ellison could install Bari Weiss, editor in chief of CBS News, atop the cable news network. (The Wall Street Journal first reported that Ellison had asked Thompson to stay on.)

“That sound you hear is a giant sigh of relief from halls of Techwood,” said a CNN producer, who was not authorized to comment, referring to the company’s Atlanta headquarters. That sentiment was shared by other CNN employees who spoke with the Guardian.

According to an announcement of the combined company’s leadership team, Weiss will also remain in her role as editor in chief of CBS News, despite some speculation about a potential change in her purview.

Thompson, 69, was brought on to take charge of CNN in 2023 after the tumultuous leadership of chief executive Chris Licht, who lacked network management experience and lasted just over a year. Thompson had previously served as director-general of the BBC from 2004 to 2012 and then as president and CEO of the New York Times from 2012 to 2020.

At CNN, Thompson has prioritized the network’s digital and streaming operations, as well as the creation of a new direct-to-consumer product called CNN All Access in October 2025. The CNN producer credited Thompson with “stabilizing” the business and helping to build its post-linear television future.

Thompson has also had his hands full with Donald Trump’s White House, which last month barred CNN – along with MS Now and Politico – from the building before a judge temporarily restored access.

A former longtime CNN producer said that Thompson’s presence would be reassuring because he is a known entity. “They know what he brings,” the person said.

When Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of CNN parent company Warner Bros Discovery closes on Tuesday, after the settlement of lawsuits aimed at blocking the deal, the company will begin the process of integrating the various media assets it has acquired.

It is unclear if, when or how CNN and CBS News will be merged, though they will share a parent company. The two networks have different corporate structures and serve different audiences. At an industry conference on 30 September, Paramount’s chief legal officer, Makan Delrahim, noted those distinctions. “CBS News is a handful of hours of programming,” he reportedly said . “CNN is 24-7. Just completely different markets.”

While both CBS News and CNN have large American audiences, CNN has a much larger international footprint, and there has been speculation that its foreign team could take precedence if the companies are merged. There is also the expectation of widespread layoffs across the entire company, including at CBS News and CNN, as part of an effort to slash costs.

And there have been concerns about whether the Ellison family, which controls a large chunk of American media and entertainment assets, could move CNN in a more conservative direction, a fear that Ellison himself has dismissed.

As part of a settlement reached between Paramount and a coalition of 12 state attorneys general last month who sued to block the deal, the company has agreed to create a five-person news editorial independence board within 180 days of closing the deal. The board will “establish guiding editorial and journalism principles for the combined entity’s news channels” and will ensure those principles are adhered to. But some employees at CNN and CBS News have dismissed the planned board, fearing it will lack teeth.

Thompson hinted at the uncertainty surrounding the merger in his memo. “I know many of you have had trepidations about this moment. That’s understandable – indeed, as I’ve hinted before, I’ve had the odd moment or two myself!” he said. “But I want to say that on the eve of the acquisition of CNN by Paramount Skydance, I find myself in a very positive frame of mind. I really do believe we’ll be working alongside a team who don’t just have real vision and real energy, but real values as well.”

Thompson told CNN employees that he would have more details to share on Tuesday.

stories.title: We're saving £100 a month into pensions for our toddler and baby - here's why
stories.summary: A growing number of parents are opening retirement funds for their children.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Richard Brain says that opening pensions for his young children means a few financial sacrifices now

Published 2 hours ago

Richard and Caitlin Brain's two children are aged just 20 months and five months respectively, yet mum and dad have already set up pensions for them.

The Brains, who live in Swansea, south Wales, are paying £50 a month into each of their kids' accounts. It's money that the children won't be able to access until they are 57, under current UK private pension fund rules. , external

So the eldest will have to wait until 2082, and the youngest until 2083.

Despite the wait, Richard, 30, is convinced that he and Caitlin, 28, are doing the right thing.

"Paying into their pensions means we can play a part in their future far beyond our own years. And the money has decades to grow."

'We don't eat out as often as we used to'

Richard's financial knowledge is explained by the fact he works for an investment firm. Caitlin is currently on maternity leave from her job working for the local council.

He earns less than £90,000 a year, while she currently doesn't have an income as she has not yet returned to work after her statutory maternity pay of £194 a week ended.

In addition to their children's pensions, Richard and Caitlin have also set up Junior ISA savings accounts for them, and pay in £60 a month per child - money the kids will be able to access when they turn 18.

The couple believe this is the best of both worlds – the ISAs could help their children with university costs, starting a business or a house deposit, while the pensions are intended to provide financial security much later in life.

Paying a combined £220 a month into their kids' funds, in addition to £200 into their own private pensions and savings, the couple say they must live more frugally than in the past.

"We're not on the breadline, but investing this money does mean doing a little less," says Richard. "We don't eat out as often as we used to, which as foodies is a pain.

"And we don't go as big for one another on birthdays and Christmas so that we can still do it for the kids."

'I want to retire earlier so this will help'

Pensions for children, also called Junior self-invested personal pensions (SIPPs), were introduced in the UK in 2001. You can pay in a maximum of £2,880 per year, which the government will then top up with £720 tax relief to make a total £3,600.

The popularity of Junior SIPPs has grown, industry figures show.

One provider, Hargreaves Lansdown, says that in the 12 months to April 2026 it had seen two and a half times as many accounts open , external as in the same period a year earlier.

Another, Fidelity, says it has seen the number of accounts more than triple since December 2023.

While giving their kids a pensions head start is a powerful incentive for some parents, how do the children themselves feel about not being able to touch the money for potentially 50 years or more?

Fifteen-year-old Hugo Thompson from Manchester seems unfazed. His parents, who work in finance, have been paying the maximum amount into his Junior SIPP for the past 10 years.

"The money invested means perhaps I'll be ahead when I'm older," he says. "So I won't have to put quite so much of my own money in! I want to retire earlier than the state pension age so this will all help."

Hugo's mother Annabel, who works in finance, also saves into a Junior ISA for him, but says she still also invests into her own pension and savings. "For me, Junior SIPPs should only be considered once you feel you have enough money of your own," she says.

Hugo Thompson is happy to wait until he is at least 57 to access the pension fund

For parents who can afford it, the money can grow substantially before the child can access it, says Jemma Slingo, a pensions specialist at Fidelity.

"Paying in £50 a month from birth, including tax relief, the family would contribute £10,800 over those 18 years. The pot could grow to around £135,000 by retirement. That's the real power of starting early - relatively modest amounts can have an exceptionally long time to compound."

It's not just British parents that are opening long-term investments for their children.

In July this year, US President Donald Trump launched a new retirement investment scheme for children called Trump Accounts.

Families, friends and employers can contribute up to $5,000 (£3,800) per year per child. The difference with the UK is that the children can access the funds from when they turn 18, although withdrawals are subject to taxes and a possible 10% penalty if made before the age of 59 and a half.

Wally Luckeydoo, a personal finance teacher at Smyrna High School in Tennessee, has opened Trump Accounts for his two children, aged four and three.

Wally Luckeydoo says he is giving his children a "financial head start"

"My dad passed away when I was very young, and my mom did everything she could to provide for us, often with just the bare minimum," says Wally.

"For much of my adult life, I have felt like I was trying to catch up financially, particularly because of significant student loan debt.

"I don't necessarily think of this as specifically saving for my kids' retirement. I think of it as giving them a head start and helping change the trajectory of our family financially."

stories.title: Texas city demands $2M for public records on Flock usage
stories.summary: Prices of public records tracking cops' use of Flock go up as backlash swells.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Prices of public records tracking cops’ use of Flock go up as backlash swells.

As bipartisan backlash against Flock grows , some cities are asking anti-surveillance advocates and media outlets to pay eye-popping fees—including charging tens of thousands or even millions—to get information about how police departments are using and potentially abusing AI-enabled camera systems that track every vehicle that passes them.

On Monday, the Texas Tribune reported that city officials in a Fort Worth suburb, North Richland Hills, asked one group to pay $2.3 million before it would fulfill a public records request for Flock data. To reach that high fee, officials claimed that searching “about a terabyte worth of communications about errors, misuse, and effectiveness of the Flock system” would take approximately 14 years of labor at a rate of $15 per hour.

Phil Mynona, who filed the request using a pseudonym on behalf of his group, the Texas Privacy Coalition, told the Tribune that the fee seemed “ludicrous” and designed to stifle his public records searches.

Mynona has sought similar records from more than 200 law enforcement agencies across the US, and he said it was impossible to predict how cities assessed fees for Flock records. Some cities provided more than 400,000 pages of documents for free, while others charged $5,000. Other groups, including a Houston news station called KPRC, have seen officials quote up to $121,000 for Flock records, the Tribune reported.

The high price tags may be hiding data that anti-surveillance groups note have triggered audits, arrests, and changes in how law enforcement uses cameras, including decisions to get rid of cameras. Many cops have been found using the cameras to stalk strangers and people in their personal lives, and so far, Flock has yet to introduce meaningful reforms to confront its stalker cop problem .

Texas is a perfect example of how increasing transparency about police use of Flock cameras works to protect the public from invasive searches that serve no lawful purpose. Last week, an ex-Texas cop, Zachary Anthony Klein, reportedly pled guilty to 100 felony counts of misuse of official information, which he agreed to do in exchange for the state not pursuing charges related to stalking several people. Klein’s Flock abuse—along with another cop’s—was outed after USA Today submitted a public records request that sparked a probe, then his arrest. Disturbed by the case, Texas Governor Greg Abbott quickly halted Flock funding and stopped issuing permits, the Tribune noted.

Additionally concerning are officials who deny requests outright. Consider that the Tribune reported that the state Department of Public Safety has sought help from “the Attorney General’s Office to allow it to withhold the entirety” of Flock data that the Texas Tribune has requested. And that denial came after DPS had already responded to an identical request seeking data from prior weeks, the Tribune noted.

Flock misuse recently ruled unconstitutional

Flock maintains that its automated license plate readers (ALPR) are designed for public safety, while courts have largely agreed that cops can reasonably access Flock databases without infringing Fourth Amendment rights. But ongoingly, there are cases dominating the headlines that show a widening web of privacy risks, including not just illegal surveillance by police but also hackers or bad actors improperly accessing data that can be used to track people’s daily movements.

Courts may start to rethink their stance on Flock, with one federal judge in Oklahoma last week ruling that a cop conducted an unconstitutional search when searching a Flock database simply because a woman’s license plate was from California,” 404 Media reported .

That judge, Sara Hill, argued that Flock’s network “is a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance,” with its ALPR technology creating a “large-scale, dragnet-type surveillance system” that should require a warrant to search.

A Flock spokesperson told 404 Media that the company had nothing to do with the case but expects Hill’s ruling to be an outlier that will likely be appealed and overturned.

Importantly, Hill’s decision does not set any precedent, but it could be influential as one of the first to recognize that Flock searches can be unconstitutional. 404 Media said they reviewed audits showing “there are currently more than a hundred thousand warrantless searches of the Flock system every month.” Sometimes innocent people are arrested, including one man jailed for a month based on a Flock alert that he argued should have itself provided the evidence cops needed to see that he was innocent and five miles away from the crime scene.

For members of the public increasingly scrutinizing Flock cameras over unconstitutional searches and other privacy concerns, it’s hard to know basic things, like where the cameras are posted, who’s looking at the footage, how often the data is accessed, and how long the data is stored.

Public records requests can help answer these questions, and sometimes police choose to voluntarily share it, using optional “transparency portals” that Flock builds. Those portals log statistics like total number of cameras, vehicles scanned, or police searches in a given area.

Flock spokesperson Andrew Smith told the Texas Tribune that the portals “give agencies a public-facing way to publish information about their [ALPR] programs, including policies, usage, and access rules to help communities better understand how the technology is being used.”

However, very few agencies seem to be opting in to the sharing. In Texas, there are hundreds of agencies using Flock cameras, and only 59 agencies use transparency portals, the Tribune reported. Of those, just 16 share data with the public.

Without courts requiring warrants or state and local officials requiring more transparency, Flock cameras will continue tracking movements in ways that the public doesn’t fully understand, advocates warn. And new privacy risks may emerge as AI makes it easier to process data across the ever-broadening network.

Michael Soyfer is a lawyer at the Institute for Justice who “has studied Flock camera abuse and is litigating several cases on Fourth Amendment grounds,” 404 Media noted. He suggested that without more transparency on how police are using the cameras, Flock may end up building tools to support some of these police misuses the public dislikes, such as automating the type of alerts used when tracking vehicle movements that have raised false suspicions or caused wrongful arrests.

“We’re seeing that repeatedly with police flagging whatever they’ll call suspicious patterns of movement. Federal agents were using ALPRs to monitor cars making day trips across the border and back to manufacture a basis to stop them, interrogate the drivers, and search them,” Soyfer told 404 Media. “I think Flock is going to automate that, using AI where cops can set alerts for those kinds of travel patterns.”

Command-line tool quickly removes Apple Intelligence from macOS 27
stories.summary: The tool can free up over 12GB of storage.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The tool can free up over 12GB of storage.

A new tool is allowing Mac users the ability again to easily turn off Apple Intelligence with one click and free up to 12GB of storage.

Unlike with previous versions of macOS, macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn’t have a toggle for turning off Apple Intelligence. That makes disabling AI features that you may not want more difficult. It also means that the AI models necessary for running Apple Intelligence will take up space on your disk , even if you don’t use them or if you go through your settings to individually find and disable AI capabilities.

In response, a developer known as Om Lahore on GitHub last week created RemoveMacAI, a command-line tool that allows macOS 27 users to “turn off Apple Intelligence on macOS 27″ in a way that is “fully reversible,” per the GitHub page . They said that Apple’s Intelligence models take up “about 12GB,” but the models can actually take up over 30GB, The Verge noted.

RemoveMacAI “turns off Siri, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, the ChatGPT extension, and all the summaries, then it deletes the models and stops macOS from downloading them again. Dictation still works because it’s a separate setting,” the developer said in a Reddit post first spotted by MacRumors .

On Reddit, RemoveMacAI’s developer said the tool is open source and further explained how it works:

It uses a configuration profile you approve in System Settings plus Apple’s own asset service, so [ System Integrity Protection ] stays on and nothing in /System gets touched directly. removemacai revert removes the profile, and macOS downloads the models again when you turn a feature back on.

The dev also said you can remove only the Apple Intelligence features you don’t want and keep the others.

Some users on Reddit have reported that the tool works, and it has 1,700 stars on GitHub as of this writing.

Interest in RemoveMacAI demonstrates the aversion that some users have to some or all of Apple Intelligence’s features, despite growing focus from Apple on AI-driven device and software upgrades in its computers and other devices .

“Reminds me of all the de-crufting you’ve always needed to do when you install Windows. Looks like we’ve gotten to the point on macOS too, where you need to run third-party scripts on a new OS installation to gain back control of your system resources and remove unwanted crapware,” a Hacker News user wrote in response to RemoveMacAI.

Although many users are happy to leverage Apple Intelligence in their gadgets, RemoveMacAI is a simple way for the rest to regain control over Apple Intelligence’s presence on their computers that Apple previously offered.

stories.title: Pentagon stops using Anthropic AI tools after blacklisting company, BBC told
stories.summary: It labelled Anthropic a "supply chain risk" in February after the firm refused to remove safety guardrails from its tools.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Defence secretary Pete Hegseth has publicly criticised Anthropic's boss Dario Amodei

Published 9 hours ago

The US Department of Defence is no longer using Anthropic's AI tools, an official has told the BBC, months after it designated the company a supply chain risk on national security grounds.

The Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the department official said in a statement on Monday.

Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk in February, and announced that the Pentagon would stop using it by late August. It is not clear why there has been a delay.

Multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that as recently as last week Anthopic's Claude model was still being used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran.

It was viewed as a critical tool for sorting through vast quantities of information, the people said. They include former US defence officials and contractors who have worked closely with the Pentagon specifically on AI.

A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment when asked about the Pentagon's statement.

The details of the department stopping all use of Anthropic's tools have not been previously reported.

The firm had been used by the US government and military since 2024 and was the first advanced AI company to have its tools deployed in government agencies doing classified work.

But earlier this year, the Pentagon pressed it to remove its safety guardrails from Claude and give the military unfettered access to its AI products.

When Anthropic refused, citing concerns of mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, Hegseth designated the company a "national security supply-chain risk" - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US.

Anthropic said the move was "unprecedented and unlawful" and has sued the Trump administration in an effort to overturn the designation.

Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge rules Published 28 August

Anthropic sues US government for calling it a risk Published 9 March

Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons Published 11 September

Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down Published 12 September

As this legal fight has played out in the courts, the Pentagon has signed contracts with other major tech companies, including Google, xAI and OpenAI.

OpenAI tools have been more widely adopted in recent months in some military departments, according to two people familiar with AI use in the defence department

The Pentagon's statement on Monday came in response to a question from the BBC about its use of Anthropic, after multiple people said in interviews that Claude was still being widely used.

It was embedded in a larger data platform used by the Pentagon called Maven Smart System, multiple sources said.

Maven, which is operated by Palantir, is the Pentagon's primary platform for organising intelligence and other data.

Lauren Kahn, a senior research analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology said that because Claude was deeply integrated into Maven it would have been difficult to remove it quickly from the system.

"The fact that it took the Pentagon until now to remove all use of Claude from across the system is indicative that these things are not just plug and play," she said.

"Once they become integrated it can be painful to remove them," added Kahn, a former US defence official.

Trump recently met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei at the White House

The BBC spoke with defence contractors who specialise in AI and have worked closely with the Pentagon, as well as former US defence officials and others familiar with the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence. Several spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.

When Hegseth initially ordered Anthropic to be phased out of government, "there was concern with moving beyond Anthropic to OpenAI" and other tools, a former senior US defence official said.

Hegseth set a six-month deadline to phase out Anthropic on 27 February, one day before the US and Israel attacked Iran.

Pentagon employees continued to use Anthropic's Claude tools, including its powerful Mythos models, "throughout the whole period of the controversy" with the company, one of the people said.

Claude was used in particular for intelligence gathering and analysis, including through Palantir's Maven system, several sources said. Palantir, a leading defence tech firm, was founded by the billionaire ally of President Donald Trump, Peter Thiel.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

'There is a possibility of human extinction,' former Anthropic employee says about AI

Sources familiar with the way the technology is used said analysts and other defence officials rely on Maven to access and organise visual data, including satellite imagery and drone footage.

The data was then fed into Claude and other large language models for tasks such as identifying potential military targets.

Officials frequently used the technology when compiling one-page briefs that were passed up the chain of command, according to a source who was given a demonstration of Maven by Palantir earlier this year.

Maven is also used by some US allies to share intelligence with the Trump administration.

Anthropic's clash with the Pentagon comes as relations with the White House appear to be warming. Trump met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei twice at the White House last week.

After one of the meetings with Trump and other technology leaders, Amodei said he still had concerns about risks posed by AI.

"How we address those risks is still under discussion," Amodei told reporters at the White House, as Trump stood by his side, but "if we work with the president, we can win safely".

Trump then proceeded to praise Amodei, saying he was "great" and "fantastic."

stories.title: Controlling the brain with light earns a physiology Nobel
stories.summary: The entire field of optogenetics traces back to light-seeking algae.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The entire field of optogenetics traces back to light-seeking algae.

Over decades of research, scientists have built up a partial picture of what specialized cells within the brain and spinal cord do. By studying how the brain develops, they could identify genes that were active in different populations of neurons and where in the brain those neurons resided. In some cases, these genes could then be used to genetically delete the neurons, allowing us to get some indication of what they might be doing, building on the information we’ve obtained from studies of brains with damaged regions.

But this approach has its limits. The brain is flexible enough to potentially adapt to the loss of some cells, and their loss early in development may alter the development of any neurons they would have normally formed connections with. It would be far more informative to activate and shut down the neurons in an otherwise intact brain.

Today’s Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine rewards three people—Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel—who developed our ability to do precisely that. Starting from studies of single-celled algae that are attracted to light, these and many other researchers built an entire field of study that we now call optogenetics: using light to alter the behavior of nerve cells marked by the activity of individual genes.

From algae to human cells

Nerve impulses are generated by proteins called ion channels, which sit in the membrane and allow charged atoms to cross it. The nervous system uses a population of ion channels that are only active under specific circumstances, like when they sense a neurotransmitter or experience voltage changes. It’s this fine level of control that allows specialized nerve cells to send impulses only under specific circumstances, keeping the brain from descending into a haze of electrical noise.

So if we want to find out what any of the multitudes of specialized nerve cells might be doing, the easiest way is to hijack this system: force the cell to send ion-based impulses when we tell it to, and see how the animal’s behavior changes.

The Nobel Committee notes that this idea was obvious enough that people tried several methods of doing so before developing optogenetics. But it turns out “the easiest way” did not mean “easy,” and most of these methods didn’t end up widely used because they involved some combination of needing to insert multiple genes, supplying the nerve cells with some very specific chemicals, or using lasers at an intensity that physically damaged the cells.

The ultimate solution, it turned out, was lurking in a single-celled algae called Chlamydomonas . The organism’s single cell is remarkably complicated, having two flagella that help it move around, and an eye spot that detects the light it moves toward. People had been studying the organism for quite some time as a model for basic biological processes.

This is where Hegemann, then working at Berlin’s Humboldt University, entered the picture. He and his coworkers managed to hook an electrode up to a Chlamydomonas and showed that exposing it to a flash of light resulted in a very rapid influx of ions, suggesting the light was triggering an ion channel to open. As other scientists started scanning the messenger RNAs made by Chlamydomonas , Hegemann spotted a couple of genes that were similar to a light-activated ion pump found in an archaeal species.

Suspecting these might be responsible for the ion fluxes in Chlamydomonas , Hegemann used RNA interference to block their activity. This did limit the flow of ions in response to light, clearly implicating these genes in the organism’s light sensing.

At that point, Hegemann started an extended collaboration with Nagel, then at the University of Würzburg, an expert in ion fluxes. They showed that one of the two genes was selective for only letting protons (which you can think of as a hydrogen ion) into the cell, while the other would allow a broad range of positively charged ions through. They were also sensitive to somewhat different wavelengths of light. The proteins also used a chemical relative of Vitamin A to sense light, just as the receptors in our eyes do. Collectively, this class of proteins is now termed “channelrhodopsins.”

Nagel was instrumental in broadening the use of channelrhodopsins, showing that the genes that encode these proteins could work everywhere from developing frog embryos to cultured human cells. He went on to show that, when active in the neurons of a small worm called C. elegans , exposing the worms to light could cause them to alter their behavior.

Lighting up the brain

Deisseroth and his coworkers at Stanford then played key roles in developing this into a broadly useful technology. They showed that the channelrhodopsins work in neurons, and the ion fluxes they trigger are transmitted as nerve impulses. They also found more members of the channelrhodopsin family, some of which are sensitive to different wavelengths of light. A version that allows negatively charged chlorine ions into the cell was also discovered, allowing researchers to selectively shut down nerve cells.

At the same time, Deisseroth and his team worked on the engineering side of the problem, developing compact light sources and small, flexible fiber optics that allowed the system to act in the brains of animals that were free to move about and behave relatively normally.

The result has been nothing short of a revolution in our ability to understand what different populations of nerve cells are doing. If we know a gene is active in a small population of nerve cells, then we can use the mouse version of that gene to activate channelrhodopsin there and start testing how light changes the behavior of the resulting mice.

We’ve described work that relies on optogenetics a dozen times or more . And the Nobel Committee cites its use in everything from understanding how memories are stored to figuring out what signals wake mice from sleep. In one amazing set of experiments they note, a research group took an area of the brain known to be needed for maternal care and showed it contained specialized cells that performed one of a long list of functions, like triggering mothers to search for their pups, or governing physical interactions with them.

Channelrhodopsins have even been used to restore limited light sensing in a patient with a form of blindness in which their rod and cone cells die off.

One of the clearest signs of how significant this development is has been the widespread adoption of optogenetics. While the three people being honored made key contributions to its development, they have only made a relatively small contribution to its use. Instead, the studies we see that rely on optogenetics are largely done by other people who recognized its utility and refined and extended it.

The award is also very timely for the US, where the current administration has been pushing for cutbacks in fundamental research and shifting funding to its priorities in applied fields like AI and quantum computing. It’s hard to imagine a more fundamental scientific question than “how does this bit of pond scum move to ensure it gets enough light for photosynthesis?” And it’s definitely the sort of question that gets asked without any sense that the answers would ultimately have practical applications.

But science’s story, again and again, has been one where seemingly trivial research has revolutionized entire fields of study and ultimately had implications for human health and technology. The Nobel Prize Committee, in honoring a clear breakthrough, has inadvertently provided us with a reminder of that story.

stories.title: Russian drones strike Ukraine’s data centers by exploiting air defense gaps
stories.summary: Russian attacks on Internet, phone services threaten Ukraine’s wartime economy.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Russian attacks on Internet, phone services threaten Ukraine’s wartime economy.

A surge in Russian jet-powered drone strikes on Ukrainian data centers has increasingly disrupted mobile phone and Internet services for thousands of people. Now Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and other government officials are warning of the need for more air defense capabilities, as such telecommunication outages could threaten Ukraine’s digital economy and undermine the country’s ongoing resistance to Russia’s invasion.

The Russian attacks on Ukrainian telecommunication infrastructure have focused on Ukraine’s capital of Kyiv since September 23, according to the nonprofit Reporters Without Borders . Ukraine’s digital transformation ministry reported that 100,000 households in the Kyiv region were temporarily experiencing Internet outages from those initial strikes—and Russia has only intensified its strike campaign against major Ukrainian data centers and mobile phone networks in recent weeks.

“Russian attacks on Ukraine’s telecommunication infrastructure are not new, with strikes and shelling previously damaging fiber optic lines, cell towers, and facilities belonging to mobile network companies,” said Tetiana Gaviuk , analyst for Europe at ACLED, in a post on October 1 . “However, the recent concentrated attacks on Kyiv’s data centers and telecom networks stand out because multiple providers and facilities were hit within days, indicating Russia’s increased pressure on Ukraine’s digital infrastructure.”

Such repeated attacks could undermine the telecommunication networks that support Ukraine’s banks, payment systems, and public services, according to warnings from officials and industry figures, as reported by The Guardian .

Russia’s strike campaign

Russia has launched mass missile and drone attacks on Ukraine’s power grid infrastructure, railroad stations, shipping ports, and even residential apartment buildings since the first year of its full-scale invasion in 2022. But such long-range strikes have become even more damaging this year, as they have exhausted Ukraine’s supply of missile interceptors—and Russia has also upgraded many of its one-way attack drones to become faster jet-powered drones that are more difficult to shoot down.

For example, Zelenskyy stated on October 4 that Ukrainian air defenses currently intercept more than 85 percent of conventional Shahed-type drones originally developed by Iran and supplied to Russia. But such interception rates fall to just 50 or 60 percent when dealing with newer and faster jet-powered Shahed drones.

Russia’s targeting of data centers is part of a broader long-range strike campaign against energy and commercial infrastructure that “aims to make civilian life in Ukraine unbearable such that Ukraine will capitulate to Russia’s demands,” according to the DC think tank Institute for the Study of War . The Russian strategy seeks to exploit Ukraine’s current air defense gaps and damage or destroy Ukrainian infrastructure during the colder fall and winter seasons.

However, Russia’s intensified strike campaign also coincides with Russian battlefield setbacks, especially with the Ukrainian military’s Operation Vivaldi having retaken dozens of square miles of territory near the vital fortress belt cities guarding eastern Ukraine. So the strike campaign arguably represents the main avenue open for Russian President Vladimir Putin to try claiming some semblance of victory nearly five years after the start of his so-called special military operation in Ukraine.

Telecommunication resiliency and alternatives

Ukraine has already moved some data centers outside the country and invested in building more underground telecommunication networks to boost resiliency, said Kateryna Chernohorenko, Ukraine’s former deputy minister of defense for digital transformation, in an interview with Breaking Defense . But she also cautioned that “you cannot move everything underground” and emphasized the need for allies to help boost Ukraine’s air defenses against Russia’s ballistic missiles and drones.

The telecommunication outages could force more local media outlets and ordinary civilians to turn to satellite-based solutions, like Starlink . Former Ukrainian government advisor Serhii Sternenko recommended that residents of Kyiv purchase Starlink terminals or similar alternatives ahead of winter.

“These repeated Russian strikes on Ukraine’s telecommunications infrastructure not only affect the work of the media, but also the Ukrainian population’s right to information,” said Pauline Maufrais and Vincent Berthier, regional officer for Ukraine and head of the technology and journalism desk at Reporters Without Borders, in a statement. “These are war crimes and their gravity is undeniable.”

This is not the only instance of data centers becoming wartime targets in the past year. When the United States and Israel first attacked Iran in February 2026, Iran’s retaliatory strikes on the Gulf region included targeting multiple Amazon data centers in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates. Amazon has since acknowledged the permanent loss of some Amazon Web Services customer data because of the data center destruction.

stories.title: F1 in Bahrain... in Malaysia: The race needed a software update to start
stories.summary: A software bug waylaid half the field and required a race reboot.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A software bug waylaid half the field and required a race reboot.

Well, it’s safe to say no Bahrain Grand Prix has been affected by torrential rain quite like the 2026 race.

For one thing, it was held several thousand miles from Bahrain itself. The ongoing war with Iran ruled such things out, so the Sepang International Circuit in Malaysia stepped in to fill its spot. One of the best examples of a late-’90s “Tilke track”—named for its designer, Herman Tilke—it’s characterized by a couple of long straights and the always-brutal tropical weather that provides one of the toughest physical challenges on the calendar. And this weekend was no exception.

Heavy rain arrived about half an hour before the start time, delaying things significantly. Although the sport has two different kinds of treaded tires for use in the rain, the full wet tire generates so much spray, and such slow lap times, that it’s essentially only useful for circulating behind the safety car. If it’s wet enough to need it, it will be too wet to see where you’re going. The intermediate tire, by contrast, has much shallower grooves and is good for racing on damp but not soaked tracks, although it quickly overheats and degrades as the track dries.

Chaos ensues

The organizers decided on two formation laps behind the safety car; circulating at lower speed would allow the drivers to get an idea of the track conditions and let their intermediate tires pump some water off the track surface, the idea went. But that didn’t take into account a bug lurking in the cars’ software.

Driving slowly behind the safety car with reduced hybrid power in some parts of the track due to the extremely wet conditions convinced several of the cars that they were being tricked into breaking a hard-coded rule meant to prevent cheating, triggering an automatic 60-second shutdown of their electric motors that caused chaos as car after car slowed for the one in front, then took varying lengths of time to reboot their systems.

“It was like the Lego race,” said Max Verstappen of Red Bull, referring back to the human-size Lego cars that F1 used for a driver parade at the 2025 Miami Grand Prix . “At some point, we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn’t understand what was going on. Then we did a lap and then I see eight other cars crawling still… I mean that’s not what you want, right, for the sport.”

The race organizers aborted the entire start. The bug had never come up in testing, and the FIA had to hastily write and distribute a software update to fix it. An hour after the first aborted start, the cars lined up on the grid again, ready to finally race.

“In wet conditions, there are some different software settings for the cars for safety reasons to reduce the power in certain sectors from the maximum to a lower level,” explained Nikolas Tombazis, head of single-seater racing at the FIA. “And this year, we’ve had very little wet weather running or none at all, almost. So it wasn’t maybe adequately checked.”

The software was developed by the FIA with the teams and engine makers. “So it’s common software for all cars,” Tombazis said. “And basically there was a combination of events between those software settings and the fact that some cars went incredibly slow during the formation lap and those entered a sort of a bug into the software which was stopping those cars to reaccelerate and to go to normal speeds.”

“And as a result of that, we had quite a few cars affected by that problem and which caused them to stop,” Tombazis said. “Perhaps I should also add that as soon as the formation lap problems happened, we understood the problem very soon afterward and we issued some an updated software to the teams. It took about sort of 20 minutes for the software to be issued. Some explanations teams had to update the software in the car. They had to ask a couple of questions and we had to make sure they all had done that work. So all of that took maybe about 20 minutes or so and so that was what caused that delay for the second start.”

(Indeed, the delay led Verstappen to joke that his team got their update applied faster thanks to their Oracle-supplied data connection.)

More chaos

The delay to the start was long enough that the rain had abated and the puddles of standing water had all drained, leading just over half the grid to gamble that it was dry enough to risk starting on either the soft or medium slick. Only nine drivers opted for the intermediate tire, including Verstappen (on pole), championship leader Kimi Antonelli, and his Mercedes teammate George Russell. Lewis Hamilton, starting second, was among those choosing to start on either the soft or medium slick tire; this was a mistake, as the formation lap proved the track was still much wetter than expected—too wet for slicks, certainly.

So it wasn’t a surprise to see the slick-shod cars quickly left behind as they struggled to put down power on the wet tarmac. Despite being on the intermediates, Verstappen got a terrible start and was left in third, behind both Mercedes.

“I was not surprised because my start was horrendous,” Verstappen said. “Again, dropping the clutch and not having power. The engine just completely died on me. But then you just have to settle in, try not to overreact as well, and just slot in, try to keep your position there. The race is long, a lot of things can happen, and step by step, I could close the gap.”

And he did, passing Russell on lap six and then closing up behind Antonelli quickly thereafter.

Meanwhile, at the back of the pack, some of the drivers who started on slicks made stops to change to the intermediates. McLaren’s Oscar Piastri was among the first who quickly began scything through the field; within a lap, he’d caught up and passed everyone who went by as he stopped. Others followed suit, though Hamilton was not among them, telling his race engineer on lap 5 that he’d gamble on the conditions coming back to suit him. It was a decision that would show the depth of experience that the seven-time world champion brings to the sport.

The race restarted on lap 13, and Verstappen pounced on Antonelli, taking the lead, with Russell following into second. Hamilton, meanwhile, was in 15th, although not for long. Within a lap, he was up to 11th. Within 10 laps of the restart, he was in 5th.

Slightly further back, another legend of the sport was also having a good day.

Fernando Alonso’s Aston Martin might have been a laughingstock at the start of the season, as it was multiple seconds slower than the cars of the frontrunners, but the Adrian Newey-designed aerodynamic update that arrived in Hungary closed some of the gap to the rest of the field. And Honda has now introduced a second power unit upgrade that has helped drivability even while at a power deficit to the others. It’s not quite as effective a package as Hamilton’s Ferrari, but Alonso began moving forward, and by lap 40, he was in 10th place, the final points-paying position.

Up front, Verstappen was building a commanding lead, and Antonelli had overtaken Russell for second, having first asked the team unsuccessfully if they’d simply tell Russell to let him by.

Extra chaos

Then Alex Albon’s Williams suffered a gearbox failure on lap 43, triggering a virtual safety car. Verstappen and Hamilton stopped for tires, followed a lap later by Antonelli, Russell, and the other Red Bull of Isack Hadjar. The broken transmission of the Williams prevented it from being easily moved, so a full safety car was declared, bunching the pack up.

The race would restart on lap 52 (of 55), but not before Russell came to a stop by the side of the track just past the pit exit on lap 50. “Another [power unit] failure, when we were on course for a pretty certain podium. It’s a tough one to take. It’s unfortunately happened too many times this season, and, yeah, this is just where we are,” Russell said after the race as he acknowledged his title chances for 2026 were over.

The final three laps were frenetic. Hamilton passed Hadjar for third, a wonderful recovery drive back to the podium after being more than a minute off the lead at one point during the race. His Ferrari teammate Charles Leclerc trailed behind, also passing the second Red Bull and fully salvaging Ferrari’s day. Ahead of the red cars, Antonelli was closing down on Verstappen but without being close enough to attempt an overtake. And Alonso was making moves, too, ending his day in eighth place, Aston’s best finish of the year.

Everyone knows this looks bad

On a chaotic day, F1’s biggest talents shone their brightest. Between them, Hamilton, Verstappen, and Alonso have 13 world championships, and this year, Antonelli has given every indication his name belongs alongside theirs, even if he does need to do something about his weakness for exceeding track limits. And the racing we got was actually rather thrilling. But some of that was still overshadowed by all the chaos that had to happen first. And everyone knows where to point the finger.

“The power units are exceptionally complicated. The more complicated you make things, the more there is to go wrong. So that is obviously something we need to bear in mind for the future,” said Russell. “It just proves that we shouldn’t have any of that stuff on the electronic side,” said McLaren’s Lando Norris.

“It is clear the regs are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the PUs, for the manufacturers. It is too complicated,” said Williams’ Carlos Sainz. “Again, my only question mark is who, five years ago, decided that this was the direction to go? We are doing the best with what we are given as a sport and as regulations. The FIA and F1 are doing the best they can with what was decided four or five years ago, but clearly what was decided four or five years ago is wrong.”

Next year, the power units will be rebalanced with more power from the V6 and less from the electric motor, with another change coming in 2028. Then it’s all change in 2031 (or perhaps 2030), when F1 will likely go back to V8s and much smaller hybrid systems .

stories.title: Mass quarantine issued in Russia after unexplained death of plague researcher
stories.summary: Unconfirmed reports have suggested there was a laboratory accident.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Unconfirmed reports have suggested there was a laboratory accident.

Roughly 200 people are under medical observation, several hospitals are under quarantine , and dozens are in isolation in Russia following the unexplained death of an infectious disease researcher at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia, in the town of Shelekhov, according to early reports of the situation on Sunday and Monday.

Researcher Darya Shipilova reportedly died last week from pneumonia of “ unknown ” cause, according to Rospotrebnadzor, a Russian public health agency.

Unconfirmed information regarding her death has swirled. Some reports have claimed she accidentally broke a test tube containing the plague pathogen, Yersinia pestis , on September 25. She subsequently fell ill, was admitted to a hospital September 29 with severe pneumonia and died overnight between October 1 and October 2. The head of the Russian region that neighbors Irkutsk, Alexey Tsydenov, initially reported that she had died of plague but later altered his statement to say she “possibly” died of the disease.

Y. pestis can cause several forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic—the latter of which can be aggressive and quickly fatal. However, the pathogen is generally easily treated by antibiotics. In the US, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that anyone exposed to the pathogen should undergo an immediate seven-day post-exposure antibiotic prophylaxis treatment. Additionally, though pneumonic plague is spread via respiratory particles from coughing, it is not considered highly infectious; it requires direct, close contact for the bacteria to be transmitted.

Former Rospotrebnadzor head Gennady Onishchenko said Friday that Shipilova’s infection was “most likely not the plague” but that there “will be no spread of this disease,” CNN reported.

Rospotrebnadzor has downplayed the incident, saying in a statement that the “epidemiological situation” in the region is stable. “No micro-organisms associated with the employee’s professional duties were detected in samples taken from the patient,” it said.

However, the agency’s current head, Anna Popova, made an unusual trip to Irkutsk on Friday, which Igor Kobzev, the local governor, described as due to a “suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection affecting a resident of the region.”

A spokesperson for the US State Department told CNN, “We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners. Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly.”

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said on Monday that it, too, is monitoring the situation “very closely.”

Kyrgyzstan, around 1,500 miles from Irkutsk, said Monday it was introducing quarantine controls at state border crossing points.

stories.title: AI glasses face their first major government crackdown
stories.summary: Norway wants time to write permanent rules for glasses that can record bystanders.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Norway wants time to write permanent rules for glasses that can record bystanders.

Norway has become the first major country to propose a temporary ban on the use of AI glasses in selected public places amid growing privacy concerns over wearable technology.

The rich Scandinavian country’s center-left government said on Monday that it would introduce a law to parliament soon on a temporary ban for places such as parks, beaches, schools, and kindergartens. It will also set up an expert group to propose permanent national rules.

“I am concerned about the introduction of powerful new technology where people risk being photographed, filmed, or recorded without their knowledge,” said Torgeir Micaelsen, Norway’s digitalization minister. A temporary ban “will give us time to conduct a thorough assessment and hold an informed debate that can lay the foundation for permanent regulation,” he said.

Governments around the world are grappling with how to regulate AI glasses—including those from Facebook owner Meta and cheaper copycat devices—amid worries that they are being used to film people without their consent, including children and women in settings such as changing rooms.

Parts of Norwegian society have already reacted with their own bans, including schools in the capital Oslo and the country’s biggest company, oil and gas major Equinor, which has banned them from its offices and offshore facilities.

Australia is considering a ban on smart glasses in certain public spaces, while courtrooms in several countries have issued bans as the use of wearable technology increases.

Norway’s government said it did not want to propose a total ban. It said that appropriate use could be where there was no risk of filming people without their consent.

It added that the proposed ban was a “high priority” and that a draft law would soon be presented to parliament.

“We do not want a society where people are concerned about hidden audio recordings, photography, and filming in places and situations where they are used to being without being monitored. Such a society can be experienced as unsafe and cause us to withdraw,” said Micaelsen.

US tech companies such as Meta, Google, and OpenAI believe wearable technology, like smart glasses, has the potential to replace mobile phones as our main gateway to AI. They believe that talking to AI—which will listen to people’s conversations and daily life—is easier than opening an app and typing in queries. Analysts at Counterpoint Research estimate consumers will spend more than $1 trillion between 2026 and 2032 on wearable devices.

But that has raised widespread privacy concerns about what such smart glasses could see or hear, and led to them being dubbed “pervert technology” by some campaigners.
